newsitem.title: JAPAN: Insurance accord seen hitting Japan non-life firms.
newsitem.headline: Insurance accord seen hitting Japan non-life firms.

text.p: The Japan-U.S. agreement on opening up Japan's insurance market will hurt the earnings of Japanese non-life insurers in the 1997/98 financial year, which starts next April, the chairman of the Marine and Fire Insurance Association of Japan said on Monday.
Takeo Inokuchi, who is also president of Mitsui Marine & Fire Insurance Co Ltd, told reporters that the non-life insurance industry would be hardest hit by the agreement.
Inokuchi said: "The non-life insurance industry has become a victim."
Under the agreement, the premiums for some fire insurance products will be cut from January 1, 1997, and this will undermine earnings for the next full business year, he added.

Under a basic deal clinched over the weekend with the United States, Japan agreed to deregulate its non-life insurance sector by mid-1998. Japan will also give insurers more freedom to set premiums for fire insurance policies.

Currently, the firms are free to set their own level of premiums for corporate fire insurance offering over 30 billion yen worth of coverage. Under the agreement, Japan will lower that threshold to policies with over 20 billion yen of cover on January 1, and to seven billion yen on April 1, 1998.

The impact of the agreement will be enormous on the non-life insurance industry because it will only be one and a half years before premiums for non-life insurance products will be liberalised, Inokuchi said. This time frame is too short for the industry to prepare for the liberalisation, he added.
Analysts said earlier on Monday that the deregulation of the non-life sector will allow firms to set a variety of rates and is expected to generate strong competition.
